quests.hint: Use 'Compared to…, this one is…' to directly contrast two options in a clear structure.
quests.explanation: 'Compared to the older model, this one is significantly better' is a clean, direct comparison. Leading with 'compared to' immediately signals a contrast is coming, making your reasoning easy to follow.
quests.situationText: A salesperson asks whether you prefer the newer smartphone model or the older one and why.
quests.sampleAnswer: Compared to the older model, this one is significantly better - the camera is sharper and the battery life is genuinely impressive. I'll take this one.
acceptedSynonyms: newer model is worth the extra cost

quests.hint: Use 'Both have their merits, but ultimately…' when comparing two equally good options.
quests.explanation: 'Both have their merits' shows intellectual fairness before stating your preference. 'Ultimately' signals you are about to give your final, considered verdict - which sounds thoughtful rather than impulsive.
quests.situationText: Your colleague asks you to compare two project proposals and say which one you would recommend.
quests.sampleAnswer: Both proposals have genuine merits, but ultimately I'd recommend Option A - the implementation timeline is far more realistic given our current team capacity.

quests.hint: Use 'The main difference between the two is…' to cut straight to the most important distinction.
quests.explanation: 'The main difference is' immediately focuses the comparison on what matters most. It is efficient, analytical, and shows you can prioritize information rather than simply listing everything you know.
quests.situationText: Your manager asks you to briefly explain how two competing software packages differ from each other.
quests.sampleAnswer: The main difference is cost versus flexibility. Platform A is cheaper to run, but Platform B gives us far more customization options for our specific workflow.

quests.hint: Use 'I've weighed up the pros and cons and I've decided to…' to present a reasoned decision.
quests.explanation: 'I've weighed up the pros and cons' demonstrates mature, analytical thinking. Following immediately with your decision makes you sound confident and clear-headed rather than indecisive or uncertain.
quests.situationText: Your mentor asks what you have decided about whether to apply for the internal promotion.
quests.sampleAnswer: I've weighed up the pros and cons carefully and I've decided to go for it. I think I'm genuinely ready for the next challenge. Wish me luck!
quests.correctAnswer: decided to go for the promotion
acceptedSynonyms: decided to go for the promotion
weighed up the pros and cons

quests.hint: When genuinely undecided, say 'I'm torn between… and… What would you do in my position?'
quests.explanation: 'I'm torn between' honestly signals genuine indecision. Asking 'What would you do?' invites the other person's perspective and makes them feel genuinely valued in the conversation.
quests.situationText: You cannot decide whether to pursue a Master's degree now or gain two more years of work experience first.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm genuinely torn between starting the Master's now or working for two more years first. What would you honestly do if you were in my position?
acceptedSynonyms: doing a Master's now or working first

quests.hint: Change a decision gracefully: 'I've had second thoughts about… and I think it makes more sense to…'
quests.explanation: 'I've had second thoughts' is a natural English phrase for reconsidering a previous decision. It is honest and self-aware, showing you have reflected carefully before changing course rather than being indecisive.
quests.situationText: You told your team you would present on Friday but have realized Monday would be far better.
quests.sampleAnswer: I've had second thoughts about presenting on Friday. Given the data we are still waiting for, Monday morning would actually make much more sense for everyone.
quests.correctAnswer: having second thoughts about presenting Friday
acceptedSynonyms: having second thoughts about presenting Friday

quests.hint: Express a professional worry: 'I'm a little concerned about the timeline on this project.'
quests.explanation: 'I'm a little concerned' is professionally appropriate for raising a worry in a work setting. It is assertive enough to be taken seriously without sounding alarmist, accusatory, or unhelpful.
quests.situationText: You are in a team meeting and genuinely worried that the deadline is not realistic given current workload.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm a little concerned about the timeline we've committed to. Given what we still need to complete, I think we might need at least one additional week to do this properly.
acceptedSynonyms: not realistic given what we still need to do

quests.hint: Share a personal worry: 'I've been a bit worried about… lately and I'm not sure what to do.'
quests.explanation: 'I've been worrying about' (present perfect continuous) correctly describes a worry that has been ongoing recently. Adding 'I'm not sure what to do' invites support rather than demanding a solution.
quests.situationText: You confide in a close friend about a health concern that has been on your mind for several weeks.
quests.sampleAnswer: I've been a bit worried about my health lately - I keep getting these persistent headaches. I'm not sure whether I should just see a doctor or wait and see.
acceptedSynonyms: been a bit worried about my health

quests.hint: Raise a budget concern: 'I'm worried about the costs here - are we sure we can afford this scope?'
quests.explanation: Raising a financial concern with 'are we sure we can afford this?' is assertive but collaborative - it invites discussion rather than blocking a decision, which is the mark of effective professional communication.
quests.situationText: You are reviewing a project proposal and notice the estimated costs are significantly higher than expected.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm a bit worried about the budget here. The projected costs are quite a bit higher than I was expecting. Are we definitely within our approved financial scope?

quests.hint: Give specific positive feedback: 'What really stood out was the way you…'
quests.explanation: Specific feedback is always more valuable than vague praise. 'What really stood out' highlights a particular strength, showing you paid careful attention and have genuinely thought about what made the work excellent.
quests.situationText: Your junior colleague has written their very first formal report and it is surprisingly excellent.
quests.sampleAnswer: What really stood out was the clarity of your executive summary. It was well-structured, precise, and genuinely easy to follow. You should be proud of that.

quests.hint: Give constructive criticism: 'One area I'd suggest working on is… Have you thought about…?'
quests.explanation: The feedback structure: start positive, then 'one area to work on' for critique, then a question. This makes critical feedback feel genuinely helpful and forward-looking rather than harsh or discouraging.
quests.situationText: Your manager asks you to give constructive feedback to a colleague after their first presentation.
quests.sampleAnswer: One area I'd suggest working on is pace - you were speaking quite fast in places. Have you thought about adding deliberate pauses after each key point? It really helps the audience absorb information.

quests.hint: Deliver balanced feedback: 'The content is strong. It might benefit from a little more…'
quests.explanation: Separating the praise ('the content is strong') from the suggestion ('it might benefit from') makes feedback feel balanced. The modal 'might' softens the suggestion, presenting it as an option rather than a criticism.
quests.situationText: You are reviewing a colleague's marketing proposal before it is sent to a client tomorrow.
quests.sampleAnswer: The content is genuinely strong and well-researched. It might benefit from one or two more concrete statistics in the opening paragraph - just to hook the reader from the very start.

quests.hint: Receive feedback graciously: 'Thank you - that's really useful. I'll work on that right away.'
quests.explanation: 'That's really useful' acknowledges the genuine value of feedback you received. Saying 'I'll work on that' shows you have accepted it positively and plan to act - the mark of a growth-oriented professional.
quests.situationText: Your manager gives you detailed, specific feedback after reviewing your quarterly performance report.
quests.sampleAnswer: Thank you so much - that's genuinely really useful feedback. I can see the areas to improve now. I'll get started on addressing them straight away.

quests.hint: Ask for clarification on feedback: 'Could you give me a specific example of what you mean by…?'
quests.explanation: Asking for a specific example shows intelligence and commitment to improvement. It transforms potentially vague criticism into actionable guidance you can actually work with.
quests.situationText: Your teacher tells you your writing 'lacks flow' but you are not entirely sure what they mean by that.
quests.sampleAnswer: Could you give me a specific example of where the flow breaks down in my essay? I want to make sure I understand exactly what to focus on improving for next time.
quests.correctAnswer: could you give me a specific example
acceptedSynonyms: could you give me a specific example

quests.hint: Respond to tough feedback professionally: 'I appreciate your honesty. I'll take some time to reflect on this.'
quests.explanation: 'I appreciate your honesty' is a mature, professional response to challenging feedback. 'I'll take time to reflect' signals serious engagement rather than defensive dismissal - a sign of genuine professional maturity.
quests.situationText: A mentor has given you some very challenging but honest feedback about your leadership approach.
quests.sampleAnswer: I genuinely appreciate your honesty - it takes courage to say that, and it's exactly what I needed to hear. I'll take some time to properly reflect before responding. Thank you.
acceptedSynonyms: exactly what I needed to hear

quests.hint: Make a professional commitment: 'I give you my word that it will be done by [day].'
quests.explanation: 'I give you my word' is a formal, powerful English commitment. It is stronger than 'I promise' in professional contexts and signals full personal accountability for the outcome you are committing to.
quests.situationText: A client is worried about whether the project will be completed on the agreed deadline.
quests.sampleAnswer: I give you my word that the full report will be on your desk by five o'clock on Thursday afternoon, without any exceptions.
quests.correctAnswer: on your desk by five on Thursday
acceptedSynonyms: on your desk by five on Thursday

quests.hint: Make a personal promise: 'I promise I'll never let this happen again. I'm truly sorry.'
quests.explanation: 'I promise I'll never…' is a sincere personal commitment in English. This phrase carries significant emotional weight and is most powerful after a mistake has hurt or inconvenienced someone you care about.
quests.situationText: You have let a good friend down by canceling plans at the last minute for the second time recently.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm truly sorry. I promise I'll never cancel on you last-minute like this again. I know how frustrating it is and you deserve better from me.
quests.correctAnswer: I give you my word it will not happen again
acceptedSynonyms: I give you my word it will not happen again

quests.hint: Make a conditional commitment: 'As long as we receive the data by Monday, I can guarantee delivery.'
quests.explanation: A conditional commitment ('as long as') is professionally honest about the dependency. It signals confidence in the outcome but clearly identifies what needs to happen first - a sign of responsible communication.
quests.situationText: Your stakeholders want a guaranteed outcome but one important factor remains outside your control.
quests.sampleAnswer: As long as we receive the client data by Monday morning, I can absolutely guarantee we will deliver everything on schedule by the end of next week.
quests.correctAnswer: as long as we receive the data by Monday
acceptedSynonyms: as long as we receive the data by Monday

quests.hint: Express professional doubt: 'I'm not entirely convinced that this approach will work as planned.'
quests.explanation: 'I'm not entirely convinced' is a diplomatically phrased skepticism. 'Entirely' softens the doubt, making it sound like a measured professional concern rather than a blunt or personal objection.
quests.situationText: In a team meeting, someone proposes a strategy that you have significant concerns about.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm not entirely convinced that this approach will scale given our current resource constraints. Could we explore one or two alternatives before committing fully?

quests.hint: Express personal uncertainty: 'I'm honestly not sure whether I'm making the right call here.'
quests.explanation: 'I'm honestly not sure' uses 'honestly' for a candid, self-aware admission of genuine uncertainty. This kind of vulnerability in English conversation builds trust and signals emotional intelligence.
quests.situationText: You are about to make a significant career decision and talk through your real doubts with a mentor.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm honestly not sure whether I'm making the right call. Part of me is genuinely excited by the challenge, but another part has real doubts about the timing of it all.
quests.correctAnswer: not entirely sure I am making the right call
acceptedSynonyms: not entirely sure I am making the right call

quests.hint: Signal risk: 'I have my doubts about this - it seems like quite a significant gamble.'
quests.explanation: 'I have my doubts' is a common and natural English expression for skepticism. Describing the situation as 'a gamble' uses metaphorical language to emphasise risk in a vivid and memorable way.
quests.situationText: A colleague proposes a bold but very risky business strategy and asks your honest opinion.
quests.sampleAnswer: I have genuine doubts, honestly. It's creative and I see the appeal, but it seems like quite a significant gamble given how tight our current budget already is.
quests.correctAnswer: have genuine doubts about this strategy
acceptedSynonyms: have genuine doubts about this strategy

quests.hint: Speculate about a cause: 'It could be that… or perhaps it's due to…'
quests.explanation: 'It could be that' is a modal expression for speculation - you are proposing a possibility, not stating a fact. This careful language prevents you from sounding certain about something you are only guessing at.
quests.situationText: Your team is trying to work out why a recent marketing campaign dramatically underperformed.
quests.sampleAnswer: It could be that the target audience was too broad, or perhaps it's down to the timing - launching just before a major bank holiday was probably not ideal.
acceptedSynonyms: timing of the launch was also off

quests.hint: Speculate about the future: 'I imagine that within ten years, we'll see significant changes in…'
quests.explanation: 'I imagine that' signals a forward-looking speculation based on observable trends. It is softer than 'I predict' and invites others to engage with your idea, making the conversation genuinely dynamic.
quests.situationText: Your English class is discussing how the world of work might be different in the next ten to twenty years.
quests.sampleAnswer: I imagine that within ten years we'll see a dramatic reduction in five-day office weeks. Four days will probably become the new standard for many industries.
quests.correctAnswer: four-day working week within ten years
acceptedSynonyms: four-day working week within ten years

quests.hint: Speculate about a person: 'I suppose she might have done that because…'
quests.explanation: 'I suppose she might have' uses two layers of tentativeness - 'suppose' signals uncertainty and 'might have' further distances the claim from established fact. Together they sound grammatically sophisticated and natural.
quests.situationText: A colleague missed an important meeting and nobody knows the reason why. You speculate carefully.
quests.sampleAnswer: I suppose she might have had a personal emergency come up at the last moment. She seemed quite stressed yesterday now that I think about it. I'll check in with her.
quests.correctAnswer: might have had a personal emergency
acceptedSynonyms: might have had a personal emergency

quests.hint: Show empathy: 'I'm so sorry to hear that. That must have been incredibly hard for you.'
quests.explanation: 'That must have been incredibly hard' uses 'must have been' to express imagined empathy. You are acknowledging what the person went through without claiming to fully understand it - which is the honest and generous thing to do.
quests.situationText: Your friend tells you they unexpectedly lost their job after five years at the same company.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm so sorry to hear that - that must have been a real shock. Five years is a long time. How are you holding up? Is there anything I can do to help?
quests.correctAnswer: must have been a real shock
acceptedSynonyms: must have been a real shock
five years is a long time

quests.hint: Offer support: 'I want you to know I'm completely here for you, whatever you need.'
quests.explanation: 'I'm here for you, whatever you need' is one of the most supportive English phrases. It is open-ended and unconditional - you are offering presence and help without specifying its form, giving full freedom to the person.
quests.situationText: Your close friend has just told you they are going through a very painful and difficult personal situation.
quests.sampleAnswer: I want you to know I'm completely here for you - whatever you need, whenever you need it. You absolutely do not have to go through this alone.
acceptedSynonyms: you are not alone in this

quests.hint: Validate feelings: 'It sounds like you're feeling really overwhelmed right now - that makes complete sense.'
quests.explanation: 'That makes complete sense' validates someone's emotional experience powerfully. It signals you understand WHY they feel as they do, which is more empathetic and meaningful than simply saying 'I understand.'
quests.situationText: A colleague vents that they feel completely overwhelmed by their current workload and management pressure.
quests.sampleAnswer: It sounds like you are completely overwhelmed right now and that makes total sense. You've been carrying an enormous amount lately. Please know you can always talk to me.
quests.correctAnswer: sounds like you are completely overwhelmed
acceptedSynonyms: sounds like you are completely overwhelmed
you have been carrying so much

quests.hint: Express pleasant surprise: 'Oh wow - I wasn't expecting that at all! That's incredible news!'
quests.explanation: 'I wasn't expecting that at all' conveys genuine surprise. 'That's incredible news!' adds warm enthusiasm. Together they make for a very natural, warm English response to unexpectedly good news.
quests.situationText: Your boss unexpectedly announces that the whole team is getting a substantial bonus this quarter.
quests.sampleAnswer: Oh wow - I genuinely wasn't expecting that at all! That is incredible news. The whole team has worked so hard for it. Thank you so much!
quests.correctAnswer: was not expecting this at all
acceptedSynonyms: was not expecting this at all
whole team has worked so hard
genuinely shocked in the best way

quests.hint: Express shock at bad news: 'That's absolutely devastating. I can't believe it.'
quests.explanation: 'Absolutely devastating' shows deep, genuine shock. 'I can't believe it' is one of the most natural English reactions to bad news and sounds completely authentic and empathetic in context.
quests.situationText: A friend tells you that their house was seriously damaged in a flooding incident last night.
quests.sampleAnswer: That's absolutely devastating. I genuinely can't believe it - you must be completely in shock right now. Please let me know what I can do to help. Anything at all.

quests.hint: React to surprising news: 'You're joking! That's completely out of the blue - I had absolutely no idea.'
quests.explanation: 'You're joking!' is one of the most natural English expressions of disbelief. 'Out of the blue' is a very common idiom for something completely unexpected. Together they create a vivid, authentic reaction.
quests.situationText: Your colleague tells you that your quietest coworker is actually a semi-professional jazz musician.
quests.sampleAnswer: You're joking! That is completely out of the blue - he seems so quiet in all our meetings. What instrument does he play? I had absolutely no idea!
quests.correctAnswer: you are joking that is incredible
acceptedSynonyms: you are joking that is incredible
genuinely did not see that coming
